title: Steering by Influence: Curvature Aware Data Weighting for Activation Steering

paper.title: Steering by Influence: Curvature Aware Data Weighting for Activation Steering
paper.abstract:
Abstract Inference-time steering offers cheap, fine-grained control over a language model’s outputs by estimating a concept’s representation in activation space and shifting activations towards it. Existing methods build these representations from activation averages over contrastive datasets. These averages incorporate unrelated concepts and noise, and are dominated by a few tokens, meaning the activation transport encodes token-level rather than thematic concepts.
In this work, we steer towards examples that most express a concept thematically, rather than towards an expectation over all. We identify these examples using influence functions, which estimate how much each data point contributes to a model’s representation of a concept. Unlike simple model activation similarity, they incorporate the curvature of the model’s loss landscape, allowing them to capture concept-relevant relationships beyond superficial token-level similarity.
We then propose influence-weighted activation transport, which uses optimal transport to steer activations of non-concept text towards those of concept text, weighting concept examples by their influence scores.
We evaluate on toxicity suppression (Jigsaw), object-based concept induction (OneSec) and truthfulness induction (TruthfulQA), outperforming existing activation-transport baselines.
We track capability after steering using perplexity and MMLU accuracy, finding that our method improves steering while largely preserving model quality. We further show that influence functions capture concept-relevant information that activation-based methods miss with the two approaches ranking data points significantly differently. Together, these results demonstrate the value of curvature-aware influence information for activation steering.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The rapid increase in size and capability of deep neural network models Cottier et al. [2024] , Kaplan et al. [2020] has moved the field from smaller, cheaply trained specialist models to large, expensive-to-train general models, requiring nation-state or frontier-lab resources to train Epoch AI [2026] . It has therefore become infeasible for most to train large general models from scratch, whether to adapt to a specific context, remove data, or introduce new capabilities. The field has therefore created a wide variety of post-training model adaptations, such as LoRA Hu et al. [2021] , quantisation Frantar et al. [2022] and continual learning Wang et al. [2024] , to adapt models without expensive re-training. Activation steering is one such cheap post-training model adaptor that seeks to control model output by directly changing activation representations of the model at inference time, underpinned by the linear representation hypothesis [ Park et al., 2023 ] . By constructing the model’s activation representations of desired or undesired concepts, activation steering moves inference-time activations towards or away from these compiled representations [ Subramani et al., 2022 , Turner et al., 2023 ] . Activation steering has been achieved by using a contrastive dataset (both with and without the desired concept/behaviour) to create a contrastive gradient via differences [ Rimsky et al., 2024 , Jorgensen et al., 2023 ] , as well as by using optimal transport maps between the two activation representation distributions as a steering map [ Singh et al., 2024 , Rodriguez et al., 2025 , Rodriguez et al., 2026 ] . In another field of model interpretability, influence functions have been used to trace compromised outputs [ Li et al., 2024 ] , modify model behaviour through training-data perturbations [ Rosser et al., 2026 ] , and identify thematically malign code [ Quinzan et al., 2026 ] based on its thematic links to other data. Using second-derivative techniques [ Koh and Liang, 2017 , Bae et al., 2022 ] , thematic links between data can be identified beyond the token level [ Grosse et al., 2023 ] . Existing transport-based methods weight every sample in a class equally [ Singh et al., 2024 , Rodriguez et al., 2025 ] , regardless of how well it encodes the concept, meaning the transport direction is noised by unrelated concepts mixed in, as well as by weak examples of the concept. Methods that do weight training data [ Nguyen et al., 2026 ] do so at the token level rather than thematically (We define our use of the term ‘thematic’ as: “the underlying concept a sample expresses, independent of its specific wording”). We bridge this gap by weighting the distributions of an affine optimal transport map, in the style of Rodriguez et al. [2026] , using per-layer influence scores for each sample, so that the map steers towards the samples that most strongly define the concept rather than towards a noisy class mean.

sections.heading: Activation Steering
sections.text: Activation steering was prompted by the linear representation hypothesis [ Park et al., 2023 ] , which holds that high-level concepts are represented by linear directions in a model’s activation space. Concepts such as refusal [ Arditi et al., 2024 ] , truthfulness [ Burns et al., 2022 , Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ] , and gender [ Belrose et al., 2023 , Bolukbasi et al., 2016 ] have all been shown to be linearly represented. Early work steered model output using expert neurons [ Cuadros et al., 2022 ] and probing techniques [ Suau et al., 2024 ] . However, neuron-based steering is unstable due to superposition [ Elhage et al., 2022 ] , as a single neuron may activate for multiple concepts, whereas population-level representations carry greater semantic information [ Zou et al., 2023 ] . Subramani et al. [2022] and Turner et al. [2023] steered using the difference between contrastive prompts, which Rimsky et al. [2024] and Jorgensen et al. [2023] extended to mean differences over contrastive prompt sets. Wang et al. [2025] constructed dynamic steering vectors based on the current activation’s proximity to linear hallucination directions. However, contrastive steering vectors are coarse and noisy due to their high dimensionality, with steering in a low-dimensional subspace proving more effective [ Huang et al., 2026 , Teo et al., 2025 ] . They are also highly sensitive to prompt tokens, even in-distribution [ Tan et al., 2024 ] , and reduce output confidence [ Huu-Tien et al., 2024 ] . All tokens in the contrastive pairs are also treated equally; Nguyen et al. [2026] address this by using contrastive gradients to select the top- k k most influential tokens. An alternative line of work learns affine transformations between class-conditional distributions. Singh et al. [2024] derive optimal affine steering functions that minimally change representations while transporting one distribution to another. Rodriguez et al. [2025] generalise this with AcT, which fits affine transport maps grounded in optimal transport theory and forms the basis of our methodology. AcT fits each layer’s map independently and sequentially; Rodriguez et al. [2026] instead optimise all intervention layers jointly using a Wasserstein loss, with a sparsity regulariser limiting the number and magnitude of interventions. Abdullaev et al. [2026] relax the single-mode assumption by modelling activations as Gaussian mixtures and transporting between clusters.

sections.heading: Influence Functions
sections.text: Originating in robust statistics [ Cook and Weisberg, 1980 , Hampel, 1974 ] , influence functions (IFs) have been used to explain model predictions and identify influential training data [ Koh and Liang, 2017 ] . Despite concerns about their reliability in deep networks [ Basu et al., 2020 ] , IFs approximate local training-point effects in function space [ Bae et al., 2022 ] . Grosse et al. [2023] demonstrate that IFs capture conceptual rather than merely lexical similarity: a query about an AI being shut down was strongly influenced by training examples involving human survival despite little token overlap, with similar effects across languages and different implementations of the same algorithm. They scale this analysis to models with up to 52 billion parameters using Eigenvalue-corrected Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (EK-FAC) to approximate inverse-Hessian-vector products, building on K-FAC [ Martens and Grosse, 2015 ] and subsequent extensions for weight-sharing architectures, reusable tooling, and low-precision training [ Eschenhagen et al., 2023 , Osawa et al., 2023 , Lin et al., 2024 ] .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments and Results
sections.text: We now compare our weighted methods against their non-weighted counterparts to test whether IF weighting produces a more effective form of steering. We experiment on two open-weight decoder-only models, Gemma-2-2B [ Team et al., 2024 ] and Llama-3.2-3B [ Grattafiori et al., 2024 ] , hereafter Gemma and Llama. Hook points are listed in Appendix H . To compute our IF weightings we build the approximate Gauss–Newton Hessian, using an approximation of the model’s training data: 100 extracts of Wikipedia articles taken from the Wikimedia dumps Foundation [] .

sections.heading: General concept Induction
sections.text: The OneSec dataset [ Scarlini et al., 2019 ] contains sentences for, object-based concepts. We use the extract of OneSec from Rodriguez et al. [2025] , covering the seven concepts { baby, balloon, book, church, cloud, flower, football }, each with ∼ 700 \sim 700 sentences. For consistency, we follow the methodology of Rodriguez et al. The judge is given the concept’s WordNet definition Fellbaum [1998] and answers yes or no . We report concept presence as the fraction of generations judged yes , p ⁡ ( yes ) p(\text{yes}) . sections.heading: Truthfulness Induction
sections.text: TruthfulQA Lin et al. [2022] contains 817 multiple-choice questions spanning 38 categories, each paired with sets of true and false reference answers. Following Li et al. [2023] , Rodriguez et al. [2025] , we use an average over a 2-fold cross-validation. For each fold, the contrastive dataset is built from the training half with D + D_{+} made of questions concatenated with a true answer, and D − D_{-} concatenated with a false answer. The held-out half is used as the test set for the steered model. sections.heading: 6 Discussion & Conclusion
sections.text: Across our experiments, we see that in most cases the inclusion of curvature information in the weighted steering of activations via optimal transport helps the induction of the concepts of truthfulness (TruthfulQA) and generic objects (OneSec), and substantially helps the suppression of the broader concept of toxicity (Jigsaw). Our first steering method, IF-Act, often achieves high scores on the truthfulness and OneSec concepts; however, this often comes at a high cost to MMLU and perplexity, placing it at a less favourable point on the steering–quality trade-off. On the other hand, IF-LinEAS often improves on LinEAS while largely preserving model quality, giving a favourable balance between steering performance and capability preservation. Interestingly, in the full results of the ablation study on whether to steer over all layers or to exclude the first and last layers, we found that while not steering on the first and last layers hurt the headline induction/suppression, it significantly helped the stability of the model, giving lower perplexity and higher MMLU scores. We hypothesise that not steering at the beginning gives the model a better chance to understand the text, and that not steering at the end leads to less volatility in the output tokens, which may aid perplexity and help the model select the right multiple-choice answer, improving MMLU scores. We leave testing this hypothesis to future work.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations & Future work
sections.text: A pattern we observed throughout our testing was that influence scores concentrate in the middle layers of the model (Appendix P ). Currently, the steering strength γ \gamma is applied uniformly across all layers. We would therefore like to extend the simple non-uniform layer steering we began with (not steering on the first and last layers), and investigate whether the per-layer IF score breakdown could be used as a signal for where, and by how much, each layer should be steered. We hypothesise that steering the middle layers more strongly will disrupt the model less, as it avoids interfering with token understanding and reconstruction at either end of the model. Future work could additionally compare methods at matched perplexity or capability levels to characterise the steering–quality trade-off directly. More broadly, we use curvature-aware influence functions as a principled signal for identifying concept-relevant steering examples. Other data-attribution or relevance signals could potentially provide complementary or similarly effective weightings, and systematically comparing such signals is an interesting direction for future work.

sections.heading: 8 Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work studies inference-time activation steering. Such methods are inherently dual-use. While they can be used to reduce undesirable behaviours or improve model outputs, the same techniques could also be used to induce undesirable behaviours. Our experiments are conducted for the purpose of understanding and evaluating activation-steering methods. Our toxicity experiments use existing datasets containing toxic language and involve generating model continuations that may contain toxic content. These generations are used solely for evaluating steering performance and are not intended for deployment or distribution. No new human-subject data is collected as part of this work.

sections.heading: Appendix C Optimal Transport background
sections.text: OT considers two distributions μ \mu and ν \nu , whose densities can be imagined as sources and sinks. The goal is to find the most efficient way to transport the source mass to the sinks by minimising a cost function (for example, the Euclidean distance c ⁡ ( x , y ) = ∥ x − y ∥ c(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert [ Villani, 2009 ] ). The transport plan Γ \Gamma dictates how many units of mass to move from each source to each sink location. Mass moved must be non-negative, Γ ⁡ ( x , y ) ≥ 0 \Gamma(x,y)\geq 0 ; all of the source mass must be moved and every sink must be filled, ∫ Γ ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ 𝑑 y = μ ⁡ ( x ) \int\Gamma(x,y)\,dy=\mu(x) and ∫ Γ ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ 𝑑 x = ν ⁡ ( y ) \int\Gamma(x,y)\,dx=\nu(y) ; and a sink can be filled by mass from multiple sources. The total cost of a plan is ∫ ∫ ⁡ c ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ Γ ​ ( x , y ) ​ 𝑑 y ​ 𝑑 x \int\int c(x,y)\,\Gamma(x,y)\,dy\,dx [ Villani, 2009 ] .

sections.heading: Appendix F Synthetic datasets
sections.text: We use LLMs in the creation of contrastive triples for defining the concepts. Specifically we use Claude Sonnet 5 Anthropic [2026] . We use the prompt: You are helping build a contrastive dataset for defining concepts. TARGET CONCEPT: {concept} Generate {n} contrastive triples. Each triple is [prefix, positive_completion, negative_completion]. Requirements: 1. PREFIX - A natural, open-ended beginning of a sentence or short passage (roughly 3-20 words). - It must NOT contain, name, hint at, or strongly imply the target concept. - It should be neutral enough that both completions read as natural, fluent continuations. - It should end mid-sentence so that the completion comes right after it (keep any trailing space). 2. POSITIVE COMPLETION - A short continuation (1-6 words) that clearly and unambiguously expresses the target concept. - The concept should be carried by the completion alone, not by the prefix. 3. NEGATIVE COMPLETION - A short continuation (1-6 words) that fits the same prefix just as naturally but does NOT express the target concept. - It should be neutral with respect to the concept, not its exaggerated opposite, unless no neutral option exists. - Match the positive completion as closely as possible in length, grammatical role, register and topic, so that the only systematic difference is whether the concept is present. 4. DIVERSITY - Vary the domains (everyday conversation, news, fiction, online comments, workplace, dialogue, instructions, etc.), sentence structures, and vocabulary. - Do not reuse the same prefix template or the same completion words more than twice. - Cover different ways the concept can show up (explicit words, implied tone, different intensities, different targets or contexts). 5. QUALITY CHECK (apply silently before answering) - Remove any triple where the prefix alone already signals the concept. - Remove any triple where the negative completion still weakly expresses the concept. - Remove any triple where either completion is ungrammatical or unnatural after the prefix. OUTPUT FORMAT Return ONLY valid JSON, with no commentary and no markdown fences. Use a single key equal to the target concept, mapping to a list of triples: { "{concept}": [ ["<prefix>", "<positive_completion>", "<negative_completion>"], ... ] }

sections.heading: Appendix G Sense check Toxicity Classification
sections.text: In these plots we use the influence scores wrt the concept of toxicity over each layer to classify data points in our toxicity and neutral datasets. Figure 4 : Here we vary the number of contrastive prompt completion pairs whilst classifying toxicity using EK-FAC and MLP parameters Interestingly we see two trends here. Firstly, the amount of new information added about a concept seems to decrease after ∼ 32 \sim 32 examples; this also may be due to single examples having more of an impact at smaller k k when averaged over all k k equally. Secondly, a recurring signal we see is that IF scores are far more valuable in the middle of the model. One possible explanation is that this is where the model does most of its higher-level processing of these concepts, rather than understanding the input at the beginning or reconstructing tokens at the end. We leave a detailed investigation of this effect to future work.

Roberts † Affiliation: Machine Learning Research Group, Department of Engineering Science University of Oxford Francesco Quinzan Affiliation: Machine Learning Research Group, Department of Engineering Science University of Oxford Abstract Inference-time steering offers cheap, fine-grained control over a language model’s outputs by estimating a concept’s representation in activation space and shifting activations towards it. Existing methods build these representations from activation averages over contrastive datasets. These averages incorporate unrelated concepts and noise, and are dominated by a few tokens, meaning the activation transport encodes token-level rather than thematic concepts. In this work, we steer towards examples that most express a concept thematically, rather than towards an expectation over all. We identify these examples using influence functions, which estimate how much each data point contributes to a model’s representation of a concept. Unlike simple model activation similarity, they incorporate the curvature of the model’s loss landscape, allowing them to capture concept-relevant relationships beyond superficial token-level similarity. We then propose influence-weighted activation transport, which uses optimal transport to steer activations of non-concept text towards those of concept text, weighting concept examples by their influence scores. We evaluate on toxicity suppression (Jigsaw), object-based concept induction (OneSec) and truthfulness induction (TruthfulQA), outperforming existing activation-transport baselines. We track capability after steering using perplexity and MMLU accuracy, finding that our method improves steering while largely preserving model quality. We further show that influence functions capture concept-relevant information that activation-based methods miss with the two approaches ranking data points significantly differently. Together, these results demonstrate the value of curvature-aware influence information for activation steering. † † footnotetext: Corresponding authors: jamesd@robots.ox.ac.uk , sjrob@robots.ox.ac.uk . 1 Introduction The rapid increase in size and capability of deep neural network models Cottier et al. [2024] , Kaplan et al. [2020] has moved the field from smaller, cheaply trained specialist models to large, expensive-to-train general models, requiring nation-state or frontier-lab resources to train Epoch AI [2026] . It has therefore become infeasible for most to train large general models from scratch, whether to adapt to a specific context, remove data, or introduce new capabilities. The field has therefore created a wide variety of post-training model adaptations, such as LoRA Hu et al. [2021] , quantisation Frantar et al. [2022] and continual learning Wang et al. [2024] , to adapt models without expensive re-training. Activation steering is one such cheap post-training model adaptor that seeks to control model output by directly changing activation representations of the model at inference time, underpinned by the linear representation hypothesis [ Park et al., 2023 ] . By constructing the model’s activation representations of desired or undesired concepts, activation steering moves inference-time activations towards or away from these compiled representations [ Subramani et al., 2022 , Turner et al., 2023 ] . Activation steering has been achieved by using a contrastive dataset (both with and without the desired concept/behaviour) to create a contrastive gradient via differences [ Rimsky et al., 2024 , Jorgensen et al., 2023 ] , as well as by using optimal transport maps between the two activation representation distributions as a steering map [ Singh et al., 2024 , Rodriguez et al., 2025 , Rodriguez et al., 2026 ] . In another field of model interpretability, influence functions have been used to trace compromised outputs [ Li et al., 2024 ] , modify model behaviour through training-data perturbations [ Rosser et al., 2026 ] , and identify thematically malign code [ Quinzan et al., 2026 ] based on its thematic links to other data. Using second-derivative techniques [ Koh and Liang, 2017 , Bae et al., 2022 ] , thematic links between data can be identified beyond the token level [ Grosse et al., 2023 ] . Existing transport-based methods weight every sample in a class equally [ Singh et al., 2024 , Rodriguez et al., 2025 ] , regardless of how well it encodes the concept, meaning the transport direction is noised by unrelated concepts mixed in, as well as by weak examples of the concept. Methods that do weight training data [ Nguyen et al., 2026 ] do so at the token level rather than thematically (We define our use of the term ‘thematic’ as: “the underlying concept a sample expresses, independent of its specific wording”). We bridge this gap by weighting the distributions of an affine optimal transport map, in the style of Rodriguez et al. [2026] , using per-layer influence scores for each sample, so that the map steers towards the samples that most strongly define the concept rather than towards a noisy class mean. 1.1 Contributions To the best of our knowledge, our novel contributions are categorised below. Additionally code for all is provided via our repository. 1 1 1 https://github.com/JDIXON-2/Concept_Activation_Transport • We introduce influence function weighted activation steering that uses curvature-corrected influence function scores to estimate how much each steering example contributes to steering at each model layer. • We propose a contrastive, length-normalised measurement function over prompt–completion triples that constructs a contrastive estimate of a concept direction in parameter space. • We use the block-diagonal structure of EK-FAC to decompose influence by layer, creating a distinct effective steering dataset at each model layer. • We replace the uniform empirical measures of transport-based steering with influence-derived masses and exploit it in both a closed-form (IF-Act) and a jointly optimised (IF-LinEAS) steering methods. Concepts such as refusal [ Arditi et al., 2024 ] , truthfulness [ Burns et al., 2022 , Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ] , and gender [ Belrose et al., 2023 , Bolukbasi et al., 2016 ] have all been shown to be linearly represented. Early work steered model output using expert neurons [ Cuadros et al., 2022 ] and probing techniques [ Suau et al., 2024 ] . However, neuron-based steering is unstable due to superposition [ Elhage et al., 2022 ] , as a single neuron may activate for multiple concepts, whereas population-level representations carry greater semantic information [ Zou et al., 2023 ] . Subramani et al. [2022] and Turner et al. [2023] steered using the difference between contrastive prompts, which Rimsky et al. [2024] and Jorgensen et al. [2023] extended to mean differences over contrastive prompt sets. Wang et al. [2025] constructed dynamic steering vectors based on the current activation’s proximity to linear hallucination directions. However, contrastive steering vectors are coarse and noisy due to their high dimensionality, with steering in a low-dimensional subspace proving more effective [ Huang et al., 2026 , Teo et al., 2025 ] . They are also highly sensitive to prompt tokens, even in-distribution [ Tan et al., 2024 ] , and reduce output confidence [ Huu-Tien et al., 2024 ] . All tokens in the contrastive pairs are also treated equally; Nguyen et al. [2026] address this by using contrastive gradients to select the top- k k most influential tokens. An alternative line of work learns affine transformations between class-conditional distributions. Singh et al. [2024] derive optimal affine steering functions that minimally change representations while transporting one distribution to another. Rodriguez et al. [2025] generalise this with AcT, which fits affine transport maps grounded in optimal transport theory and forms the basis of our methodology. AcT fits each layer’s map independently and sequentially; Rodriguez et al. [2026] instead optimise all intervention layers jointly using a Wasserstein loss, with a sparsity regulariser limiting the number and magnitude of interventions. Abdullaev et al. [2026] relax the single-mode assumption by modelling activations as Gaussian mixtures and transporting between clusters. Influence Functions Originating in robust statistics [ Cook and Weisberg, 1980 , Hampel, 1974 ] , influence functions (IFs) have been used to explain model predictions and identify influential training data [ Koh and Liang, 2017 ] . Despite concerns about their reliability in deep networks [ Basu et al., 2020 ] , IFs approximate local training-point effects in function space [ Bae et al., 2022 ] . Grosse et al. Our first steering method, IF-Act, often achieves high scores on the truthfulness and OneSec concepts; however, this often comes at a high cost to MMLU and perplexity, placing it at a less favourable point on the steering–quality trade-off. On the other hand, IF-LinEAS often improves on LinEAS while largely preserving model quality, giving a favourable balance between steering performance and capability preservation. Interestingly, in the full results of the ablation study on whether to steer over all layers or to exclude the first and last layers, we found that while not steering on the first and last layers hurt the headline induction/suppression, it significantly helped the stability of the model, giving lower perplexity and higher MMLU scores. We hypothesise that not steering at the beginning gives the model a better chance to understand the text, and that not steering at the end leads to less volatility in the output tokens, which may aid perplexity and help the model select the right multiple-choice answer, improving MMLU scores. We leave testing this hypothesis to future work. 7 Limitations & Future work A pattern we observed throughout our testing was that influence scores concentrate in the middle layers of the model (Appendix P ). Currently, the steering strength γ \gamma is applied uniformly across all layers. We would therefore like to extend the simple non-uniform layer steering we began with (not steering on the first and last layers), and investigate whether the per-layer IF score breakdown could be used as a signal for where, and by how much, each layer should be steered. We hypothesise that steering the middle layers more strongly will disrupt the model less, as it avoids interfering with token understanding and reconstruction at either end of the model. Future work could additionally compare methods at matched perplexity or capability levels to characterise the steering–quality trade-off directly. More broadly, we use curvature-aware influence functions as a principled signal for identifying concept-relevant steering examples. Other data-attribution or relevance signals could potentially provide complementary or similarly effective weightings, and systematically comparing such signals is an interesting direction for future work. 8 Ethics Statement This work studies inference-time activation steering.
